title: 3-Read Friday #76: Teaching Transformations, Cognitive Load, and Paper vs E-Readers
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's 3-Read Friday #76 brings together instructional design, memory theory, and reading research. Kris Boulton continues his atomisation series on Unstoppable Learning with a detailed look at how to teach 'transformations' - tasks with an input, a prompt, and an unrestricted range of possible responses - using a tight sequence of three carefully chosen examples followed by extensive checking for understanding, in contrast to the finite, restricted-response 'categoricals' covered in earlier posts. Dylan Kane distils Cognitive Load Theory down to a single accessible idea - 'students learn what they think about' - tracing the theory from Sweller's original number-puzzle experiment through worked examples, fading, split-attention, and the expertise reversal effect, arguing that most abstract jargon around intrinsic/germane/extraneous load obscures rather than illuminates the underlying principle. Alex Quigley synthesises recent University of Valencia research comparing print and digital reading, finding that print still edges out screens for text comprehension, particularly for younger children still developing as readers, while older readers can benefit more from digital formats. Barton's framing threads these together as three practical syntheses of research that a busy teacher (or parent) can act on directly.
points: Kris Boulton's teaching sequence for 'transformations' (tasks with an unrestricted range of correct responses, unlike finite-answer 'categoricals'): three carefully sequenced examples, roughly 20 seconds each, followed by extensive checking for understanding.

Boulton's example shows how a substitution transformation can be taught with just three worked examples and no analogies or long explanations - 'job done' - because the examples themselves, adhering to setup, difference, and sameness principles, do the teaching.

Dylan Kane's distilled version of Cognitive Load Theory: 'students learn what they think about' - reframing intrinsic, germane, and extraneous load as restatements of this one underlying idea rather than three separate technical concepts to memorise.

Kane traces CLT from Sweller's original 1982 number-puzzle experiment (where participants never noticed a solvable pattern because the process was too mentally taxing) through the worked-example effect, fading, split-attention, and the expertise-reversal effect.

Alex Quigley's research synthesis: University of Valencia research across two decades finds print reading generally out-performs screens for text comprehension, with the effect strongest for young children still developing as readers and reversing somewhat for older, secondary-age readers.
quotes: I find Kris' Unstoppable Learning newsletter fascinating. In this post he introduces how to teach Transformation Atoms. Three carefully chosen examples, 20 seconds, and then lots of checking for understanding.
If you want a 5-minute summary of the key concepts in Cognitive Load Theory, then this is for you. There's even a comment on the post from Paul Kirschner as an added bonus.
